title: The Rock, the Toll and the Legend
subtitle: Bacharach on foot → downstream through the gorge → Boppard at sunset
heroKicker: One town, one boat, one sunset
intro: An afternoon in a medieval wine town, then the last boat of the day down the most famous stretch of the Rhine — Kaub, Oberwesel, the Loreley, St. Goar — landing at Boppard for sunset. Two fixed times all day: off the hill at 4:30, on the pier at 4:55.

dayGlance.title: Bacharach on foot
dayGlance.sub: 2:10 PM — land, eat, the town, then the climb. Off the hill by 4:30.

dayGlance.title: Down the gorge
dayGlance.sub: 5:15 PM — Kaub, Oberwesel, the Loreley at 5:57, St. Goar at 6:00.

dayGlance.title: Boppard & the light
dayGlance.sub: 6:50 PM — a Roman fort, then sunset at 8:24 on the promenade.

actsLede: Three acts: the town, the water, the light.

acts.label: Act 1 · Bacharach on foot
acts.tagline: The whole afternoon in one small town.
acts.narrative:
You land at 2:10 with 2 hours 45 minutes before you have to be on the pier. Enough for the town and the hill, but keep moving.

Do lunch and the market square as one thing — you won't eat again until Boppard at about seven. Then the 1368 house and the church, both quick. The climb is what you're protecting: 15 minutes up to the chapel, 15 more to the castle, about 20 back down. Leave the top at 4:30 and you're on the stage at 4:55 with five minutes spare. If you're behind, stop at the viewpoint below the castle — same view, saves the last climb.

acts.label: Act 2 · Down the gorge
acts.tagline: The whole gorge from the water, in evening light.
acts.narrative:
Going downstream you're with the current, so the gorge unrolls quickly: Kaub at 5:25, Oberwesel at 5:41, the Loreley at 5:57 and St. Goar at 6:00.

Evening is the right time to do this. The light is low and warm on the vineyard terraces, and you've already spent the afternoon standing in the town the Loreley legend was written about — so when the rock comes up you can point back upstream and say so. Stay on deck the whole way; it comes faster than you think.

acts.label: Act 3 · Boppard & the light
acts.tagline: A Roman wall, a river bend, and the sun going down.
acts.narrative:
Off at Boppard around 18:50. It's a bigger, more workaday town than Bacharach and it has the one thing Bacharach hasn't: a standing Roman fort wall in a public park, free, that you can walk up to.

Then the promenade. Boppard sits on the sharpest bend in the Rhine, so the view opens right up after the narrow gorge. Golden hour 19:40, sunset 20:24. Sign off there, then Koblenz and a direct train to Brühl.

kit: Phone or camera plus a spare battery — you're out from 1 PM until after dark
A clip mic or AirPods — the boat deck is windy and loud
Shoes for a steep 25-minute climb on cobbles and steps
A layer for the evening — it drops fast once the sun goes off the gorge
Card and some cash: KD ticket, lunch, wine. The chapel and the hill are free.
preTrip: Buy the KD ticket at the St. Goar kiosk when you arrive — a single upstream leg doesn't need pre-booking
At lunch, check DB Navigator for the last useful train to Köln, then set an alarm 30 minutes before it
Ask at the Stahleck desk whether day visitors can use the terrace — if not, the public viewpoint below is free and it's the same view
Screenshot this plan — phone signal in the gorge is patchy
goldenRule: One fixed time in the whole day: 16:55 on the Bacharach KD stage for the 17:15 boat. There is no later one.

days.planHeader: Town, then water, then sunset · until late

planNote.text: Landing Bacharach 2:10 PM with 2 hours 45 minutes before the pier. That is enough for the town AND the climb, but it is not loose — the hill is 15 minutes up to the chapel and 15 more to the castle, and about 20 minutes back down. EAT IN BACHARACH: dinner in Boppard won't be until roughly 7 PM. Do lunch and the market square as one 35-minute slot. Two numbers that matter: leave the top of Stahleck at 4:30, and be standing on the KD stage at 4:55 for the 5:15. There is no later boat. Buy the ticket through to BOPPARD, not St. Goar. Downstream the gorge unrolls fast: Kaub 5:25, Oberwesel 5:41, the Loreley 5:57, St. Goar 6:00, into Boppard about 6:50 — confirm that arrival at the kiosk, it's my estimate not their timetable. Sit on the RIGHT going down for the Loreley. Escape hatch if you change your mind on the water: the boat calls at St. Goar about 6:01 and you can get off there instead — Rheinfels is shut by then (closes 6, last admission 5) but the climb and the castle terrace are open, and trains run home from there too. Then Boppard: Roman fort while there's light on it, dinner, and the promenade for golden hour at 7:40 and sunset at 8:24. Home is easy and late — Boppard to Koblenz about 15 minutes (last around 22:51), then a DIRECT train Koblenz to Brühl, about 53 minutes (last around 23:26).

planArrival.title: Brühl by about 10:15 PM if you leave Boppard at 8:45
planArrival.note: And you can leave much later if you want — the last connection out of Boppard is around 22:51. Check DB Navigator, but there's no squeeze tonight.

loreley.name: The Loreley
loreley.angle: The legend is 225 years old, not medieval
loreley.story: Forty minutes down from Bacharach, on your right, and the low evening light is the best you'll get on it all day. Everyone films the rock; almost nobody knows the story is a modern invention — and it was written about the town you just spent the afternoon in.
facts: A wall of slate 132 metres above the water, and right here the Rhine squeezes down to 113 metres wide — the narrowest point on the whole navigable river. Fast, deep, and it genuinely used to wreck boats. The danger was real. The girl was not.

Nobody in the Middle Ages told stories about a woman on this rock. A writer called Clemens Brentano invented her in 1801, in a ballad called 'Zu Bacharach am Rheine' — Bacharach on the Rhine. He set it in the town we spent this afternoon in, back upstream.

A German poet called Heinrich Heine wrote the famous version in 1824, and it became one of those poems every German child learns at school. Here's the part people don't know: when the Nazis took power they wanted it gone, because Heine was Jewish. It was too popular to ban — so they kept printing it in schoolbooks and credited it to 'author unknown'.

routeCard.sub: From the deck, right-hand side · about 5:57 PM
routeCard.note: Seen from the deck — nothing to navigate to. The map pin is the Loreley rock itself if you want to look it up. Going downstream the Loreley is on your RIGHT, about 40 minutes out of Bacharach. This is the one you came for — do not be inside when it arrives.

planCard.todo: THE shot of the day. Be on deck from 5:50. Film the rock, then say the 1801 line — the poem was set in Bacharach, where you've just come from. That's your whole story in one sentence.

oberwesel.name: Oberwesel & Schönburg
oberwesel.angle: The town that kept its towers
oberwesel.story: About fifteen minutes past Kaub, on your left. Oberwesel is called the town of towers and you can count them from the water. Schönburg sits above it — and its story is the whole valley's story in miniature: built to tax the river, burned by the French, left as a ruin, bought back.
facts: Oberwesel kept 16 of its 21 medieval wall towers. Most Rhine towns pulled theirs down in the 1800s to make room for roads and the railway — this one didn't, and you can see the whole defensive ring from the boat.

Schönburg up there wasn't a house, it was a walled village. At its peak in the 1300s about 250 people from 24 different families lived inside it at once — the castle got subdivided between heirs until it was basically a stone tower block.

In 1689 it was burned down by the army of the French king Louis XIV, who sent his soldiers up this valley to torch it town by town. It stayed a ruin for about 200 years, until a German-American businessman spent a fortune rebuilding it before 1914. The town bought it back off his son in 1950.

routeCard.sub: From the deck, left-hand side · about 5:41 PM
routeCard.note: Seen from the deck — nothing to navigate to. The map pin is Schönburg, above Oberwesel if you want to look it up. Going downstream, Oberwesel is on your LEFT. Schönburg is the castle on the hill above the town.

see: The medieval wall and its towers
The Liebfrauenkirche, red against the hill
planCard.todo: Swap to the right-hand rail. Count the towers on camera — it's a better line than reciting the number.

kaub.name: Kaub — Pfalzgrafenstein & Gutenfels
kaub.angle: A castle parked in the middle of a river to take your money
kaub.story: Ten minutes after you leave Bacharach, on your right. A stone ship moored midstream with a castle on the hill behind it — a two-part trap, and the clearest possible picture of what every castle in this valley was actually for.
facts: That white castle sitting in the middle of the river is called Pfalzgrafenstein, and it was built in 1326 by the man who was king of Germany at the time, Ludwig of Bavaria. It had exactly one purpose: a chain stretched across the water, and a toll. Pay, or you don't go past. It was still taking money off passing boats until 1867.

And it was never taken and never destroyed — the only castle on this river you can say that about. Everything else here got burned at some point. It survived because it sits on a rock in a fast river and nobody could be bothered.

One more thing happened right here. Napoleon had spent years conquering most of Europe, and in 1813 he finally lost a massive battle in Germany and began retreating home to France. On New Year's night, a general from Prussia — the state that later grew into Germany — chased him across the Rhine at this exact spot, over a floating bridge of boats tied to that island. Fifty to sixty thousand men, fifteen thousand horses and 182 cannon, over several days.

routeCard.sub: From the deck, right-hand side · about 5:25 PM
routeCard.note: Seen from the deck — nothing to navigate to. The map pin is Pfalzgrafenstein, mid-river at Kaub if you want to look it up. Going downstream now, so Kaub is on your RIGHT. It comes up about ten minutes after casting off.

planCard.todo: Comes up fast — stay on deck from the off. Get it wide first, then talk over it: the chain, the toll, never taken.

old-town.name: The old town & the walls
old-town.angle: Wine money that never got knocked down
old-town.story: Bacharach is small enough to walk in twenty minutes and it still has almost its entire medieval wall. That's the unusual bit — most Rhine towns demolished theirs in the 1800s for roads and the railway. Here they just built around it.
facts: Nearly the whole medieval town wall is still standing, with its towers and gates. Walk out to the edge and you can put your hand on it. Most towns this size lost theirs 200 years ago.
The name: you'll be told it comes from 'Bacchi ara' — the altar of Bacchus, the Roman god of wine. That's a lovely story somebody invented much later. The wine part, though, is completely true.

Bacharach was one of the biggest wine names in Europe. Wine from all over the region got shipped out from this quay under Bacharach's name, because that name sold better than the name of wherever it actually came from. Everything you're looking at was paid for by that.

routeCard.sub: Marktplatz and the walls · 3:30 PM · free
routeCard.note: Lunch stop as well as a sight. Anywhere on the market square. Keep it to 35 minutes — the hill is the thing you don't want to rush.

walkPoints.name: The market square
walkPoints.story: The centre of the old town, on Oberstraße. Everything in Bacharach is within a few minutes of here.
walkPoints.todo: Start here. Eat, and film the square while you wait.

walkPoints.name: Altes Haus & Oberstraße
walkPoints.story: The 1368 house, two minutes up the main street.
walkPoints.todo: The postcard shot of the town.

walkPoints.name: The Rhine quay & KD pier
walkPoints.story: Where the wine left from, and where your boat goes from at 5:15.
walkPoints.todo: Walk down and look at it now so you know exactly where you're going at 4:55.

planCard.todo: This slot is lunch AND the square — do both together. EAT NOW: the next food is Boppard at about 7 PM, nearly five hours away. Order quickly, film the square while you wait, then get moving.

altes-haus.name: Altes Haus (1368)
altes-haus.angle: The postcard, and why it's still standing
altes-haus.story: The oldest house in town and the shot everyone comes for. It's what people call half-timbered — you can see the dark wooden beams criss-crossing the front with pale plaster filled in between. Worth thirty seconds on how that actually works, because it explains why a building that visibly leans has been fine for six and a half centuries.
facts: Built in 1368 — the oldest house in Bacharach. It's been standing for well over 650 years and it's a restaurant now.

Those criss-crossing beams aren't decoration — the wooden frame is the entire structure of the house, and everything between the beams is just filling. It's a skeleton, not a wall. That's why it can lean and twist as the wood moves over the centuries and still hold itself up.
In 1689 French troops blew up the castle and the chapel on the hill above. Down here, the houses came through. This one has outlived that war and every one since.

routeCard.sub: Oberstraße 61, Bacharach · 4:00 PM · free from outside
routeCard.note: Two minutes off the market square. Best light on the front is later in the afternoon, which is when you'll be there.

planCard.todo: Two minutes from the square. Clean front-on shot, then the line about the frame being the whole structure. Ten minutes of filming, no more.

st-peters.name: St. Peter's Church
st-peters.angle: Watch the architecture change as you look up
st-peters.story: Two hundred years to build, and you can see every one of them. Start at the bottom with the heavy round arches and follow your eye up until they go pointed. It's a building that changes style halfway through, in public.
facts: They started it around 1100 and didn't finish until the 1300s. Look at the bottom: round, heavy arches — that's Romanesque. Now look up: pointed arches, taller windows — that's Gothic. Same building, two hundred years apart.

The main hall you walk into — the long tall bit, which architects call the nave — is four storeys high. That is unusually tall, and unusually expensive, for a church in a town this small. Wine money again.

It's a Protestant church, and has been for roughly 500 years. Before that, western Europe had one single Catholic church, until a huge religious split called the Reformation broke it in two. The rule that ended the fighting was blunt: whichever side the local ruler picked, everyone living in his territory had to follow. The ruler here picked Protestant — so the town became Protestant.

routeCard.sub: Blücherstraße, by the market square · 4:20 PM · free
routeCard.note: Right on the market square, a minute from where you eat. Interiors on the Rhine usually shut around 6 PM.

planCard.todo: Quick one — in, slow tilt up the nave, out. The arches change from round to pointed as you look up and the shot explains itself.

wernerkapelle.name: The Wernerkapelle
wernerkapelle.angle: The prettiest ruin on the hill is a monument to a lie
wernerkapelle.story:
It's on the path up to the castle, so you pass it whether you plan to or not. Don't film it as scenery. It is a beautiful unfinished stone shell — pointed arches, empty windows, no roof — and it exists because of an accusation that got people killed. The honest thirty seconds you spend on that will be the strongest part of the video.

Say it simply, don't editorialise, don't linger. Then keep walking.
facts: In 1287 a boy was found dead near here. Jews were blamed, on the basis of what's called a blood libel — the false claim that Jews murdered Christian children to use their blood. It was never true. Not here, not anywhere.

What followed was a wave of massacres — mobs going through Jewish streets killing people — right along this river and the river Moselle next door. Entire communities were wiped out. This chapel was begun in 1289 to honour the dead boy as a saint, and people were still working on it in the 1430s. It was never finished.

And this isn't safely buried in the past. The Catholic Church kept that boy on its official list of local saints until 1963. A stone carving showing the murder that never happened, on the sister chapel downriver at Oberwesel, only came down in 1970.

routeCard.sub: On the castle path above the town · 5:55 PM · free, open ruin
routeCard.note: About 15 minutes uphill from the market square, directly on the way to the castle. Steps and a steady climb from here on.

see: Empty window frames against the sky
planCard.todo: Fifteen minutes uphill from the square. Shoot it, then say the 1287 story straight and plainly. Thirty seconds. Then keep climbing.

stahleck.name: Burg Stahleck
stahleck.angle: Blown up, forgotten for 200 years, now a youth hostel
stahleck.story: Twenty-five minutes of steady climbing from the town and the view arrives all at once. The castle is the seat of the men who ran this stretch of the Rhine, and what happened to it afterwards is almost funnier than its history.
facts: Twelfth century, and it belonged to the family who ran this entire stretch of the Rhine. Their title was Count Palatine — which sounds grand and just means a count who governed on the king's behalf. It made him one of the most powerful men in Germany. And that castle you saw sitting out in the river? Pfalzgrafenstein. The name literally means 'the Count Palatine's rock' — same title, same job: control the river, take the money.
French soldiers blew it up in 1689 — the same army that burned Schönburg and wrecked the chapel you just walked past. It sat as a heap of rubble for over two hundred years.
It was rebuilt in the 1920s and it's been a youth hostel ever since. You can sleep in a Rhine castle for about the price of a pizza — and the terrace has the best view on the Middle Rhine.

routeCard.sub: Above Bacharach · 6:40 PM · 15 min further up from the chapel
routeCard.note: Another 15 minutes of steps up from the chapel. LEAVE THE TOP AT 4:30 — 20 minutes down, 5 to the pier, boat at 5:15 and there is no later one. Running late? The viewpoint just below the castle has the same view and saves you the last climb.

planCard.todo: THE HARD TURNAROUND IS 4:30. Get the reveal of the view on camera the moment you arrive, say your piece, and start down at 4:30 whatever happens. It's 20 minutes down and 5 to the pier.

bacharach-pier.name: Bacharach — boarding the boat
bacharach-pier.angle: The one fixed time left in the day
bacharach-pier.story: This is the day's one hard deadline. The 17:15 is the last boat down, so there's no second chance at it. Be standing on the stage at 16:55. Buy the ticket to BOPPARD, not St. Goar, and check with the kiosk what time it actually gets in.

routeCard.sub: KD Anlegestelle Bacharach · be there 16:55 · boat 17:15
routeCard.note: Five minutes down from the market square. Buy a ticket through to Boppard and confirm the arrival time at the kiosk — my estimate is about 18:50 but they have the real timetable.

planCard.todo: Hard deadline. Ticket to Boppard. Then get a seat on the LEFT going down for the Loreley.

st-goar-water.name: St. Goar & Rheinfels, from the water
st-goar-water.angle: The castle you were supposed to start at
st-goar-water.story: St. Goar and the biggest castle ruin on the whole river, taken from the water — which is a better angle on it than you'd ever get standing in the town. Rheinfels is the huge ruin on the left bank; Katz and Maus are the two small castles on the right.
facts: That enormous ruin on the left is Burg Rheinfels. It was once the biggest castle on this river, and in 1692 it held out against a French army of around 28,000 men — the only castle on the Middle Rhine that didn't fall that war.
It survived the siege and then lost anyway: about a century later, in 1797, French troops simply blew it up. What you're looking at is roughly a third of what used to be there.

The two castles on the other bank are nicknamed Katz and Maus — cat and mouse. Rival lords built them within sight of each other, and the bigger one got named 'the cat' because it sat there watching the little one.

routeCard.note: Seen from the deck — nothing to navigate to. The map pin is Burg Rheinfels at St. Goar if you want to look it up. Rheinfels on your left, Katz and Maus on your right going downstream. The boat calls here about 18:01 — this is your last chance to get off short of Boppard if you'd rather.

see: St. Goar and St. Goarshausen facing each other
planCard.todo: Rheinfels is enormous and it reads much better from the river than from the road. Get it wide, and tell the siege story while it's still in frame.

boppard-town.name: Boppard — the Roman fort & old town
boppard-town.angle: A Roman wall you can walk up to, for free
boppard-town.story: You land about ten minutes' walk from the middle of town. Boppard is bigger and less chocolate-box than Bacharach, and it has something Bacharach hasn't: a genuine Roman fort, standing, in a park, that you can walk right up to and touch.
facts: The Romans built a fort here in the 300s AD, when this river was the hard border of their empire — everything on the far bank was outside it. The wall was about eight metres high with 28 towers, and big stretches of it are still standing in a park in the middle of town.
It's one of the best-preserved Roman forts anywhere on this river, it's in the open air on Angertstraße, and it costs nothing to walk in.

The twin-towered church on the market square has Roman baths underneath it — they found them digging in the 1960s. The Romans were here, then a church went up on top, and the town just kept building on the same spot for 1,700 years.

routeCard.sub: Old town & Archäologischer Park · about 10 min from the landing stage · free
routeCard.note: Roman fort on Angertstraße, open air and free. Market square and the Severuskirche are two minutes further.

planCard.todo: Eat here if you're hungry — plenty on the market square. Film the Roman wall while there's still direct light on it.

boppard-sunset.name: The Rhine promenade at sunset
boppard-sunset.angle: Closing shot — and the biggest vineyard on the river
boppard-sunset.story: The promenade runs right along the water and the town sits inside the Rhine's biggest bend, so you get a long open view in both directions. Golden hour starts 7:40 and the sun goes at 8:24. This is your ending.
facts: Boppard sits on the sharpest bend in the whole Rhine — the river does a near U-turn here, which is why the view opens up so wide compared to the narrow gorge you just came down.

That slope of vines across the water is the Bopparder Hamm: 75 hectares, the largest single vineyard on the Middle Rhine, and almost all of it Riesling. Same grape, same slate, same river as Bacharach.
And that's the day: a wine town in the afternoon, a castle above it, and the whole gorge from the water in the best light there is.

routeCard.note: Sunset 8:24 PM, light until about 9. It cools down fast by the water.

planCard.todo: Closing shot. Film the light first, talk second. Long steady wide of the bend for the outro.

boppard-bahnhof.name: Boppard Hbf → Brühl
boppard-bahnhof.story: Boppard station is a few minutes from the promenade. Change at Koblenz and there are direct trains all the way to Brühl.

routeCard.sub: Boppard Hbf · a few minutes from the Rheinallee
routeCard.note: Boppard → Koblenz is about 15 minutes and runs late (last around 22:51). Koblenz → Brühl is roughly 53 minutes and DIRECT, with the last one about 23:26. Total around 75–85 minutes. Loads of slack — check DB Navigator for exact times.

planCard.todo: Nothing left to film. Change at Koblenz, direct train to Brühl from there.

coldOpen.title: Cold open
facts: The hook: 'the most famous rock in Germany was made famous by a poem — and the poem is set in this town, right here'
What this is: an afternoon in Bacharach, one of the best-preserved medieval towns on the Rhine, then the last boat of the day down the gorge in evening light.
The promise: 'and we'll be sailing right under that rock at about six o'clock'

signOff.title: Closing sign-off
facts: Where you are: on the sharpest bend in the Rhine, watching the sun go down over the biggest vineyard on the river
The shape of the day: a wine town at two, a castle above it at four, the whole gorge from the water at six, and the sun going down at half eight.
The ask: like, subscribe — and where should the next one go?

talkTipbox: Assume your viewer knows none of this — and assume you don't either until you've said it out loud once. Every single time a name comes up, give one plain line on who or what that is before you carry on: not 'the Count Palatine' but 'the man who ran this stretch of river for the king'. Same for places, same for dates. Three facts a stop, and you only need the one that grabbed you. What happened, when, and why it's surprising. The Wernerkapelle is the exception — say that one plainly, no flourish, and don't rush it.
goldenRules: Be at the Bacharach pier at 16:55. The 17:15 is the last boat down — there is no later one.
Eat in Bacharach. Next food is Boppard at about 7 PM.
Buy the ticket through to BOPPARD, not St. Goar. Confirm the arrival time at the kiosk.
Going downstream, sit on the LEFT: that's the side for the Loreley and for St. Goar.
Loreley at about 5:57. Be on deck by 5:50 — this is the one you came for.
Leave the top of Stahleck at 4:30. Twenty minutes down, five to the pier — that's the whole margin.
Boppard: Roman fort first while there's light on it, then the promenade for sunset at 8:24.
Home is late and easy — Koblenz then a direct train to Brühl. No rush tonight.
outro: A wine town on foot, the whole gorge from the water at golden hour, and the sun going down at Boppard.
